title: Particles
subtitle: Grade 4 Science
objectives: Describe the particle model for solids and liquids.
Understand the difference between materials, substances and particles.
Know that particles are in constant motion, even when in a solid.
Use the particle model to explain the properties of solids and liquids.
Describe and explain how some solids can behave like liquids (e.g. powders), referring to the particle model.
Know that models are not fully representative of a real world situation and/or scientific idea.

beats.say: What is a spoon made of? What is water made of? What are you made of?
The same answer every time: particles, far too small to see.
Everything is made of particles: bits far too small for any eye to see.
A spoon, water, the air, you. All of them are made of particles.
So scientists use a model: a picture of an idea, drawn so you can see it.
This is the particle model. Forty balls in a box, standing for the real thing.
In a solid the particles are packed tightly in rows. Every one touches the next.
They cannot move about. But they vibrate: they jiggle on the spot.
Because they hold their rows, a solid keeps its shape. A brick stays a brick.
Do the particles in a block of ice stop moving? No, they do not.
They vibrate all the time. Only a little, but always.
Now heat the solid. Heat gives the particles energy, so they vibrate harder.
Heat it more and they break out of their rows. The solid has melted.
In a liquid the particles still touch, but they slide past each other.
That is why a liquid flows and takes the shape of its container.
Cool it and they slow down and lock back into rows. The same particles all the way through.
Scientists keep three words apart: material, substance and particle.
A material is what a thing is made of. Wood is a material, and a mixture of substances.

at.made: what a thing is made of

beats.say: A substance is one pure kind of stuff, the same all the way through. Water is one.
A particle is one of the tiny bits a substance is made of.
Pour sand into a cup and it takes the cup's shape, like a liquid.
But sand is a solid. Look at one grain through a lens.
The grain keeps its shape. Inside it the particles are packed in rows.
So what slides is not the particles. It is the grains, rolling over each other.
Salt, sugar and flour are powders too: solids that pour.
The particle model is useful, and it is not a photograph.
Real particles have no colour. The green is for us, so we can see them.
They are far smaller than the picture, and they come in many kinds and shapes.
The model shows forty. One drop of water has more than you could count.
In a solid the particles sit in rows and vibrate. In a liquid they slide.
They never stop moving, and heat makes them move more.
A powder pours because its grains roll, not its particles.
And the model is a picture of an idea, not a photograph.
